If you sell toys on Amazon US, the CPC is the document that decides whether your listing survives. It is also the document most often submitted wrong.
This is not legal advice. Requirements change — confirm the current rules with a CPSC-accepted lab before you ship.
What a CPC actually is A Children’s Product Certificate is a self-issued document. The importer or manufacturer issues it — not the testing lab. The lab produces the test report; you turn that report into a certificate.
That distinction is where most sellers fail. They send Amazon the lab’s report and assume it is the CPC. It is not, and Amazon’s compliance team will reject it.
A valid CPC names:
The product and the specific model/SKU it covers The US importer or domestic manufacturer responsible The date and place of manufacture The date and place of testing The CPSC-accepted third-party lab that performed the test Each rule the product was tested against, with the citation Contact details for the records custodian If any of those is missing, it is not a CPC.
Which rules a toy is tested against For a toy sold in the US, a CPC normally cites:
Rule What it covers 16 CFR 1250 (ASTM F963-23) Toy safety: mechanical, physical, flammability, heavy metals 16 CFR 1303 Lead in surface coatings (90 ppm) 16 CFR 1307 Phthalates (8 restricted, 0.1% each) 16 CFR 1501 Small parts — choking hazard for under 3 16 CFR 1500.50–.53 Use and abuse testing (drop, torque, tension) ASTM F963-23 is the current version. A certificate citing F963-16 or F963-11 is out of date and can be rejected on that basis alone.
The five rejection reasons we see most 1. The certificate is not tied to the ASIN. Amazon wants the model number on the CPC to match the listing. A generic “plush toy” certificate covering a whole factory’s output does not clear a specific listing.
2. The lab is not CPSC-accepted. Only labs accepted under CPSC’s programme can do children’s product testing. A certificate from a domestic Chinese lab without that acceptance is worthless for US import.
3. The importer field is blank or wrong. If you are the importer of record, your company name must be on it — not the factory’s, not your agent’s.
4. Age grading does not match the listing. A product tested as 3+ but listed as 0+ is a mismatch, and Amazon treats it as a compliance failure rather than a typo.
5. The test date predates a material change. Changed the paint supplier, the fabric, or the mould? The old report no longer covers the product.
What it costs and how long it takes For a straightforward toy, third-party testing to F963 plus CPSIA rules typically runs USD 300–800 per SKU and 5–10 working days, depending on how many colours and materials are involved. Complex products with electronics, batteries or multiple fabrics cost more.
A factory that already sells into the US usually has reports for its stock items. If they cannot produce one within a day, they probably do not export to the US regularly — which is itself useful information.
The trap: certificates that exist but do not cover your order A factory shows you a CE certificate and a CPC. Both look official. Then you read them:
The CE certificate is an EN71 test report from 2019, for a product with the same name but a different size The CPC names a different importer — the factory’s previous US customer The model number is the factory’s internal code, not your SKU None of these will clear Amazon. Always ask for the test report, not just the certificate. The report has the sample photos, the test dates and the actual measured values; the certificate is a one-page summary that anyone can retype.
What to ask your factory for Before you place a deposit, request:
The full test report (PDF, not a scan of a certificate) The lab’s CPSC acceptance number Confirmation of which SKU and which materials were tested Whether any component comes from a different supplier — paint, eyes, filling, batteries Point 4 matters more than buyers expect. If the eyes are bought in from another factory and that factory changes its supplier, your report may no longer be valid even though nothing about your order changed.
Where this fits in a sourcing relationship A sourcing agent who ships toys to the US should be able to tell you, before you order, which lab the factory uses and whether the report covers your SKU. If they cannot, they are moving boxes, not managing compliance.

Buyers routinely ask for “the CE certificate” when they need four different documents, and for the wrong market. Here is what actually applies where.
Not legal advice. Rules change, and your lab or notified body is the authority for your specific product.
The map Market Standard Who issues the document European Union EN71 (parts 1–3) under Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC You self-declare, backed by a test report and technical file European Union (2024 onwards) GPSR — Regulation (EU) 2023/988 You, plus a named EU responsible person United States ASTM F963-23 + CPSIA rules CPC issued by the importer, based on third-party test report United Kingdom EN71 accepted alongside UKCA You self-declare Japan ST Mark (voluntary, widely required by retail) Third-party inspection body Korea KC Mark Safety certification body Australia / NZ AS/NZS ISO 8124 Self-declaration with test report EN71: three parts, not one EN71 is the European toy safety standard, and it is modular:
EN71-1 — mechanical and physical properties: sharp edges, small parts, cords, drop and tension tests EN71-2 — flammability: how fast materials burn EN71-3 — migration of elements: 19 heavy metals that can leach from materials a child mouths A report that only covers EN71-1 is not a complete EN71 report. When a supplier sends “EN71 certified” and the document is eight pages covering only physical tests, ask for parts 2 and 3.
CE marking is a declaration, not a certificate There is no such thing as an official “CE certificate” for toys in the sense most buyers imagine. CE is the manufacturer’s self-declaration that the product meets the directive. What backs it up is a technical file containing:
The test reports Risk assessment Design and manufacturing drawings Material declarations from sub-suppliers Instructions and warnings The declaration of conformity itself The declaration of conformity must name the manufacturer and, for imports, the EU importer. Retailers and customs ask for this file, not a certificate with a logo.
The GPSR rule most importers miss Since 13 December 2024, the General Product Safety Regulation applies in the EU. It is not a toy-specific standard, but it adds requirements that break more shipments than EN71 does:
An EU responsible person must be identified — a natural or legal person established in the EU — on the product, the packaging, the parcel, or an accompanying document. For online sales, the information must also appear on the listing.
If you are a non-EU seller shipping to EU customers, you need this. A Chinese factory cannot be your responsible person. Neither can a freight forwarder, unless they formally accept that role.
GPSR also brings traceability requirements and mandatory reporting of accidents through the EU’s Safety Business Gateway. Ask your supplier whether their packaging already carries a responsible-person block; if they export to the EU regularly, it will.
US: the ASTM and CPC combination The US route is a third-party tested report plus a self-issued certificate. ASTM F963-23 is the current toy standard; the CPSIA rules on lead and phthalates are the other half. Details on what gets rejected are in our CPC guide.
The key difference from the EU: in the US, the lab must be CPSC-accepted and the testing is mandatory for children’s products. In the EU, you can in principle self-declare without third-party testing — though no serious retailer will accept that, and it is a poor idea for anything a child mouths.
Japan, Korea, UK in one line each Japan — the ST Mark is voluntary by law but effectively required by retailers. Testing is done by an approved inspection body and takes several weeks; budget for it early if Japan is a target market.
Korea — the KC Mark is mandatory for toys and requires certification through a Korean safety body, with the importer often acting as the applicant. This is genuinely harder to arrange from outside Korea.
UK — EN71-based CE marking continues to be accepted alongside UKCA. Do not let a supplier charge you twice for a “new UK certificate” without checking whether the CE file already covers it.
What to actually request from a factory The full test report for your SKU, not a sample report Which parts of EN71 (or F963) are covered, by number The declaration of conformity, with the importer field visible For the EU: confirmation of who is named as responsible person under GPSR Material declarations for paint, eyes, filling and any electronic components Point 5 is where certificates quietly stop being valid. A report covers the materials tested on the date tested. Change the paint supplier and the old report describes a product that no longer exists.
How this affects sourcing decisions Compliance cost is per SKU and per market, and it does not shrink with order size. A 300-piece trial order carries the same test cost as a 30,000-piece one, which is why small orders to regulated markets are disproportionately expensive — and why a supplier who already holds reports for a stock item is worth a premium.
For the operational side — what we check before shipping — see quality control and compliance.

A factory quotes 1,000 pieces. You need 300 to test the market. Most buyers respond by asking for a discount on a smaller order — which is the one approach that never works.
MOQ is not a negotiating stance. It is a cost calculation. Once you know what drives it, you can change the inputs instead of arguing about the output.
Why the number is what it is A toy factory’s MOQ usually comes from one of four costs:
Driver Typical trigger Raw material minimum Fabric, vinyl or resin sold in fixed roll/batch sizes Machine setup Injection moulding, printing, sewing line changeover Printing / packaging Cartons and colour boxes have their own minimums Quality control AQL sampling needs a minimum lot to be statistically meaningful So when a factory says 1,000, ask which of the four is binding. The answer determines which lever to pull.
If it is packaging, the MOQ on the product may be far lower — factories often bundle the carton minimum into the unit MOQ out of habit.
Four levers that work 1. Standard colours and materials. Custom Pantone matching on fabric usually forces a full roll purchase. Accepting the factory’s existing stock colour can cut MOQ by half or more. Ask: “What colours are you already running this month?”
2. Plain packaging for the trial order. A white box with a sticker instead of a printed colour box removes the printing minimum entirely. Print the retail box from order two, once you know the product sells.
3. Combine SKUs, not volumes. Three designs at 300 each is often acceptable where one design at 900 is not, because the factory spreads setup across the run. This is the single most effective tactic for a first order.
4. Pay the setup cost separately. If the binding constraint is a mould or a print plate, offer to pay that cost as a one-off line item. A USD 400 setup fee to unlock a 300-piece order is often better than committing to 1,000 units of an unproven product. Confirm in writing who owns the tooling afterwards — in our terms the buyer does, once it is paid for (see how to order).
What does not work “We’ll order more next time.” Every buyer says this. Factories discount it to zero.
Asking for the small order at the large-order price. The price at 300 units is legitimately higher per unit. Expect 10–25% above the 1,000-piece price and treat that as the real cost of testing.
Going straight to a smaller factory. A factory with a 100-piece MOQ is usually a workshop, not a manufacturer — no export licence, no test reports, and a quality ceiling you will hit on order two.
Negotiating on Alibaba chat only. The person answering chat is a salesperson whose commission depends on order value. Ask for the production manager’s view on setup cost; the answer is different.
When to accept the higher MOQ Sometimes 1,000 is correct. If the product is a proven category (push-pop fidgets, standard plush mascots), the per-unit saving at 1,000 versus 300 usually exceeds the cost of holding the extra stock — especially once you count the second freight booking you avoid.
Run the arithmetic: (unit price at 300 − unit price at 1,000) × 300 versus the carrying cost of 700 extra units. For fast-moving novelty items, the higher MOQ wins more often than buyers expect.
A workable script for the first message We are evaluating this product for [market]. Our trial order is 300 pieces across three designs, with a reorder within 90 days if sell-through is good. Two questions: which of the material, mould, printing or packaging minimums is driving your 1,000-piece MOQ, and what would the unit price be at 300 with stock colours and plain packaging?
That message gets a useful answer because it gives the factory a reason to solve your problem rather than defend a number.
After the trial order The thing that actually lowers MOQ permanently is a track record. A factory that has shipped you twice, on time, with no quality claims, will take a 300-piece order without being asked — because the risk calculation has changed. This is why the first order is always the expensive one, on every route, whatever the MOQ says.

Roughly half of the suppliers presenting themselves as factories on marketplaces and trade shows are trading companies. That is not automatically a problem — some trading companies are excellent, and many factories sell through them deliberately. It becomes a problem when you are paying factory prices for an intermediary, or when a quality issue needs someone who can walk onto the production floor.
These nine checks take about a week and cost almost nothing.
The documents 1. Business licence (营业执照) Ask for the unified social credit code (统一社会信用代码). It is a public identifier and can be checked on China’s National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System. What you are looking for: does the registered scope include manufacturing of toys, or only sales?
2. Export licence A company without an export licence cannot ship in its own name and will route your order through a third party. That is a layer you should know about.
3. Product liability insurance Rarely asked for and very informative. A factory that carries it has exposure to Western retailers and has thought about recalls.
4. Test reports in the factory’s own name Not “our client tested it”. If a factory has never held a report in its own name, it has never been the responsible supplier to a regulated market.
The physical evidence 5. A video call with the machines running This is the single most useful check. Ask for a walk-through at a time you choose, with the line running. Specific requests that are hard to fake:
Pan from the entrance sign to the production floor without cutting Show the moulding machines with the counter reading Show finished cartons with a visible shipping mark Show the QC area and the inspection records on the desk A trading company will offer a pre-recorded video, or a call from an office. A factory will just walk outside.
6. Ask where the product is actually made If the answer is “our partner factory”, you are talking to a trading company. Then ask which factory, and whether you can visit it. The answer tells you whether the relationship is transparent or extractive.
7. Capacity arithmetic Ask: how many sets per day, on how many lines, at how many shifts? Then compare with your order and lead time. A factory quoting 500,000 units in 20 days with two machines is either lying or planning to subcontract.
The commercial signals 8. How they price a small order A real factory will quote a higher unit price for 300 pieces and explain why. A trading company will often quote the same low price and then discover problems later. A suspiciously flat price across volumes is a warning.
9. Who answers the technical questions Send a technical question — material grade, mould material, drop-test height, carton compression. If every question routes back to “the engineer will confirm”, that is normal for a large factory. If the answer arrives as a copy-paste with no adaptation to your product, note it.
The two questions that reveal the most “Which of your customers in our market can we speak to?” Many factories will decline, and that is legitimate — customer confidentiality is real. But how they decline is informative. “We cannot share names, but here is the market and the volume we ship there” is a professional answer.
“What went wrong on your last shipment, and what did you change?” A factory that answers “nothing” is either new, lying, or not paying attention. A good answer names a specific problem — a colour batch, a carton failure, a late raw material — and a process change.
What an audit does not tell you A passed audit is a snapshot. Factories change staff, lose key customers, and take on too much work in peak season. The most common failure mode is not a bad factory — it is a good factory that is overbooked in September and lets your order slip.
This is why the inspection before shipment matters more than the audit before the order. See quality control for what we check at each stage.
Practical sequencing Documents first — a week, costs nothing, eliminates the obvious mismatches Video call — 30 minutes, eliminates half of what remains Sample order — the only test that matters Third-party inspection on the first bulk shipment — non-negotiable for retail and Amazon Audit in person once you are ordering regularly Skipping straight to step 3 is why buyers lose deposits. The documents in step 1 are free and public.

Every buyer sourcing toys from China faces the same three options: buy on Alibaba, hire a sourcing agent, or deal with a factory directly. The advice online is usually written by someone selling one of the three.
This page compares all three on cost, control and risk — including where an agent is the wrong choice.
The short answer Your situation Best route One SKU, under 500 pcs, testing a market Alibaba with Trade Assurance 3+ SKUs from different factories, or Amazon FBA Sourcing agent You already know the factory and have a QC team Direct Custom mould, your own artwork, branded packaging Agent or direct — never a marketplace First ever import, no inspection experience Agent The rest of this page explains why.
What each route actually costs The sticker price is not the real price. Below are typical ranges for a toy order in the USD 5,000–30,000 range. Your numbers will differ, but the shape of the difference is stable.
Cost line Alibaba Sourcing agent Direct factory Unit price Baseline −5% to −15% −10% to −20% Agent commission — 3–8% of order value — Inspection You arrange (USD 250–350/day) Usually included You arrange Consolidation Not possible Included Not possible Payment risk Trade Assurance Agent holds funds Bank transfer, no recourse Your time High Low Very high The agent’s commission is usually paid back by the lower unit price and the fact that inspection is already in the service. Where the agent loses is small orders: on a USD 3,000 order, a 5% commission plus a minimum fee can wipe out the saving.
Where Alibaba wins Alibaba is genuinely good at three things, and it is dishonest to pretend otherwise.
Price discovery. You can see 40 factories quoting the same product in an hour. No agent can replicate that speed.
Trade Assurance. Payment is held until you confirm receipt. For a first order with an unknown supplier, this is real protection, and it is the reason most buyers start here.
Small trial orders. Many suppliers accept 50–100 pieces because they want the repeat order. Agents usually cannot match this, because their own minimum economics do not work below a few thousand dollars.
Where Alibaba breaks down is after the first order. The platform is optimised for transactions, not for a supply chain: no consolidation across suppliers, no factory audit, and — critically — the supplier you negotiated with is often a trading company that subcontracts the actual production.
Where a sourcing agent wins An agent earns their commission in four places.
They know which entity is actually producing. On a marketplace, the account holder and the factory are frequently different companies. An agent in Yiwu can walk into the workshop, count the injection moulding machines, and tell you whether the quote came from the people who make the product.
They consolidate. If you buy plush from one factory, fidget toys from another and packaging from a third, you either pay three sets of freight and three sets of export paperwork, or someone combines them into one container. That consolidation is often worth more than the commission.
They cover compliance. CE, EN71, ASTM F963 and CPC documentation is not optional for EU and US retail, and Amazon will reject listings without it. An agent who has shipped these categories knows which labs the factories already use and what the reports must contain.
They absorb the language and the follow-up. The unglamorous part: chasing a factory that promised photos on Tuesday, catching a colour mismatch before 20,000 units are printed, and knowing which excuse means “the line is down” versus “we took another order.”
The trade-off is dependence. A bad agent is worse than no agent, because you lose visibility and pay a margin for it.
Where buying direct wins If you have already found a factory you trust, have someone on the ground for inspection, and order enough volume to justify a dedicated mould and a direct relationship, the agent is a cost with no remaining function. At that point, negotiate direct.
The mistake is jumping to direct too early. Buyers typically try this after two or three successful orders, discover that the “factory” contact was a salesperson who has now left, and end up back with an agent — this time with a quality problem to fix.
The risks nobody puts in the comparison table Quality drift after the first order. The sample was perfect; order three is not. This happens on every route. What changes is who catches it, and whether they catch it before the container leaves.
The trading-company layer. Roughly half of “factories” on marketplaces are trading companies. That is not automatically bad — some are excellent — but the price should reflect it, and it usually does not.
Compliance documentation that does not survive an audit. A CE certificate with the wrong model number, or a CPC issued to a different importer, will fail at customs or at Amazon. Ask for a report you can read, not a PDF with a logo on it.
Payment exposure. Bank transfer to a factory you have never visited is the single most common loss in this business. Trade Assurance or an agent’s escrow removes most of it.
How to decide in ten minutes Answer these four questions:
How many suppliers? One → Alibaba or direct. Three or more → agent. Is it custom? Moulds, your artwork, branded packaging → agent or direct. Do you need compliance documents for retail? Yes → agent, unless you have your own QC. Order value? Under USD 5,000 → Alibaba. Over USD 20,000 → get quotes from all three. If you answer Alibaba to all four, use Alibaba. It is the right tool, and we tell buyers that when it is true.
Frequently asked questions Is a sourcing agent cheaper than Alibaba? Not always. On orders above roughly USD 10,000, the lower unit price plus free inspection usually offsets a 3–8% commission. Below that, the commission often costs more than it saves.
Can I use an agent for only part of the order? Yes. The most common arrangement is agent-managed production plus factory-direct purchasing for one or two simple items, consolidated into the agent’s shipment.
Does an agent replace an inspection company? No. An agent’s in-house QC is a filter, not a certificate. For retail and Amazon, keep a third-party AQL inspection on the first shipment of every new SKU.
How do I verify a factory without visiting? Ask for the business licence (统一社会信用代码), the export licence, and a video call walking through the production floor with the machines running. A trading company will struggle with the third request.
Figures above are typical ranges for toy orders in 2026 and are not quotes. For our own terms — payment schedule, tooling ownership, inspection standard and claim window — see how to order.

If you’ve ever designed a toy idea on paper and wondered how to turn it into a real, sellable product, OEM manufacturing in China is your answer. OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) toy production in Yiwu and surrounding regions has matured into a precise, efficient ecosystem that can take your concept from a sketch to container-loads of finished product in 3–6 months.
This playbook walks through every stage, with real costs, timelines and pitfalls we’ve learned from 13 years managing OEM toy projects for B2B buyers worldwide.
What OEM Means In the toy industry, OEM means you design or specify a product, and a factory manufactures it exclusively for you. Unlike ODM (Original Design Manufacturer) where you modify an existing factory design, true OEM starts from zero — your drawing, your mold, your specifications. This is how successful private-label brands like Melissa & Doug, KidKraft and thousands of Amazon private-label sellers developed their products.
Finding the Right Factory Not all toy factories can handle OEM work. Many Yiwu factories focus purely on stock items with existing molds. You need a factory that:
Has an in-house mold-making facility or works with a reliable mold partner Has at least 3 years of OEM toy experience (ask for case studies) Employs a full QC team (not just a single inspector) Can show you test reports from products they’ve already made Is located within Zhejiang or Guangdong (where the toy supply chain is concentrated) Expect 2–4 weeks of sourcing, auditing and shortlisting before you select a partner. This is the most important decision — choose wrong and you’ll lose months on revisions and waste thousands on rework.
Sampling & Tooling Once you’ve selected a factory, the OEM process moves through four stages:
1. Prototype (1–2 weeks) — your factory’s design team creates 3D renders and a hand-made or 3D-printed prototype. This validates size, material choices and basic structure before investing in expensive tooling.
2. First article sample (2–4 weeks) — the factory makes 10–50 production-like units. This is your chance to check colors, materials, assembly and safety features. Most projects require 2–3 rounds of revisions here. Budget $200–$600 for these samples including international shipping.
3. Tooling (3–6 weeks) — steel injection molds are machined. Molds for toys cost $1,500–$8,000 each depending on complexity (countless small parts like building blocks require multi-cavity molds at the higher end). The mold fee is one-time and usually amortized into your per-unit cost for the first 5,000–10,000 pieces.
4. Pre-production run (1–2 weeks) — 100–500 trial units to validate the mold, production line assembly and packaging before full mass production.
Quality Control OEM toys fail most often not at the design stage but in mass production, when factory staff cut corners on materials or assembly speed. Your QC protocol should include:
First-off inspection: when the first 10 units come off the line, check every dimension and safety feature Mid-production check: inspect random units every 2–4 hours during production AQL Level II final inspection: before packing, 125 units out of every 10,000 get a full visual, dimensional and function check Post-pack audit: verify packaging, labels and barcodes match your requirements For high-volume OEM runs, we recommend keeping an inspector on-site during production — the extra $350/day (Guangdong) or $250/day (Zhejiang) pays for itself in reduced defect rates.
Shipping & Logistics Most OEM toy shipments go via sea from Ningbo or Shanghai — the ports are within 2–4 hours of major Zhejiang toy factories. Budget 25–35 days sea freight to EU/US West Coast, 35–45 days to US East Coast or Latin America.
Key options:
FOB Yiwu: cheapest, you handle international shipping CIF destination: factory books and pays for sea freight and basic insurance DDP door-to-door: factory or agent handles everything including customs and delivery to your warehouse — most popular for Amazon FBA sellers Toy shipments are light — a 20-foot container typically holds 5,000–15,000 toy units depending on size. Full containers (FCL) offer better rates than less-than-container (LCL), but most small OEM buyers start with LCL and graduate to FCL once they have volume.
Real-World Timeline A typical OEM plush toy project timeline:
Week 1–2: factory selection, audit Week 3–4: 3D renders, prototype Week 5–7: sample revisions (2 rounds) Week 8–12: mold making Week 13: pre-production run Week 14–18: mass production + QC Week 19–20: consolidate, ship Week 21–24: sea freight to EU/US Total: ~24 weeks from first sketch to first units in your warehouse. Budget an extra 4 weeks for delays (tooling issues, material shortages, shipping congestion).
OEM toy manufacturing in China is a powerful growth engine for B2B brands — but only when managed properly. Rushing factory selection, skipping sample revision rounds or cutting corners on QC will cost you more in rework than you save upfront. Take your time, work with experienced partners, and your OEM project will deliver a sellable product that grows your business.

Toy safety certification isn’t optional. If you’re importing toys into Europe, the US or UK, missing the right certification means customs rejection, product recalls or even legal liability. For Amazon sellers, non-compliant listings get suppressed within hours of detection. This guide breaks down the four most important certification frameworks you need in 2026.
Why Compliance Matters Every year, tens of thousands of toys are recalled globally due to safety violations — small parts that pose a choking hazard, lead-based paint, or banned phthalate plasticizers beyond legal limits. Beyond the obvious risk to consumers, non-compliance hits businesses hard: customs seizures, Amazon listing removal, bad reviews, and in some jurisdictions, criminal penalties for knowing violations.
The good news: most Yiwu toy suppliers already have baseline certifications for their standard products. For custom OEM work, you’ll need to budget for third-party testing as part of your development timeline.
CE & EN71 for Europe CE marking is the EU’s primary product safety label. For toys specifically, CE marking means the product complies with EN71 — the main European toy safety standard. EN71 covers physical hazards (choking, strangulation, sharp edges), chemical safety (heavy metals, phthalates), and electrical safety for battery-powered toys.
Key facts:
EN71 is the de-facto standard for toys sold in the EU, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland Phthalate limits are strict: 0.1% total for the six regulated phthalates Newborn and baby toys face additional requirements under EN71-3 GPSR (General Product Safety Regulation) came into force December 2024, adding online marketplace obligations and product traceability requirements For importers: you are legally responsible for CE compliance, not just your supplier. Keep test reports on file for 10 years.
ASTM F963 for the USA ASTM F963 is the US equivalent of EN71. It’s enforced by the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) and covers similar categories: physical hazards, heavy metals (total lead ≤100ppm), and phthalates (≤0.1% for certain toys).
Since 2022, all children’s products including toys require a Children’s Product Certificate (CPC) — a document you issue as the importer, backed by actual test results from a CPSC-accepted third-party lab.
CPSIA (Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act) requirements you need to track:
Lead ≤100ppm total in all surfaces and substrates Phthalate bans for toys intended for children under 12 Tracking labels on every toy and packaging Age-grading compliance (no small parts for 0–3 year olds) GPSR & UKCA for UK The UK left the EU’s CE framework in 2021 and now requires UKCA marking for toys sold in Great Britain. The safety standards remain broadly aligned with EN71, but the administrative process is separate — you need a UK-based Responsible Person to handle compliance documentation.
The General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR) is newer — it applies across the EU and UK starting December 2024. It mandates:
Product safety information page (PISP) for every product sold online Traceability records linking each product batch to its manufacturer Mandatory product contact information on packaging and online listings Digital product passports for certain regulated categories Third-Party Testing For stock items, ask your Yiwu supplier for copies of their third-party test reports. Reputable factories test every batch with SGS, TÜV or Bureau Veritas and keep reports on file.
For custom OEM work, budget $800–$2,500 per product for full EN71/ASTM testing. This takes 4–6 weeks, so factor it into your development timeline. Never skip testing to save costs — one recall can cost ten times the testing fee.
Quick Checklist Confirm your target market’s certification requirements Request copies of test reports from your supplier Issue CPC (US) or appoint Responsible Person (UK/EU) Apply GPSR traceability requirements for all online listings Keep all documentation for 10 years minimum Compliance isn’t a box-ticking exercise — it’s a core part of responsible toy sourcing. Working with a Yiwu agent who understands certification frameworks saves you from costly mistakes and keeps your products moving through customs without delay.

Key Toy Categories Yiwu’s toy suppliers cover every category imaginable:
Plush & stuffed toys — the largest category, with 300+ factories producing everything from keychain-sized mascots to life-size promotional figures Educational & STEM toys — building blocks, science kits and early learning products, many with CE/EN71 pre-certification Fidget & sensory toys — the fastest-growing segment since 2021, with push-pop bubbles, stress toys and ADHD aids RC & electronic toys — budget 1:24 scale cars, drones and light-up novelty items Inflatable & outdoor toys — pool floats, beach balls and promotional inflatables using 0.3mm+ thick vinyl How to Find Suppliers There are three main paths:
Visit the trade market. Phase 1 of Yiwu International Trade City has the largest concentration of toy booths. Bring a translator, business cards and a USB drive for exchanging factory catalogs. Most booths represent 2–5 factories, so ask about direct factory visits before committing.
Use B2B platforms. Alibaba.com and Made-in-China.com have thousands of Yiwu-listed toy suppliers. Filter by “Verified Gold Supplier” and request factory audit reports before ordering samples. Be wary of suppliers with generic product photos and no company location details.
Work with a local agent. A reliable sourcing agent based in Yiwu will save you months of trial and error. They maintain direct factory relationships, can negotiate 30–50% lower MOQs, and handle on-site QC during production.
Avoiding Common Pitfalls The biggest mistake new buyers make is ordering blind. Always:
Request and verify factory licenses. Business license, ISO 9001, and toy-specific safety certifications should be verifiable through government databases. Order samples before bulk. Even small 50-piece test orders reveal quality issues, packaging problems and shipping delays. Inspect before shipment. AQL Level II pre-shipment inspection catches the defects that will anger your customers. Clarify Incoterms. FOB Yiwu is standard; beware suppliers quoting EXW who expect you to handle local transport and export customs. Working with a Sourcing Agent A good sourcing agent provides end-to-end service: supplier shortlisting, price negotiation, sample management, factory QC, consolidation and DDP shipping. The best agents have bilingual staff on the ground and maintain relationships with 200+ verified factories. For most buyers, working with a local agent delivers better prices, better MOQs and avoided shipping delays.
Yiwu toy sourcing rewards preparation. Come with clear specifications, reasonable MOQ expectations and a budget for samples, and you’ll find suppliers that deliver quality toys at prices that let you compete in Amazon, retail and wholesale channels.

Reports are issued per product, per factory batch, by an accredited third-party laboratory — and we send you the real document for the SKU you are evaluating.
Which tests apply to your product Testing scope depends on the product, not the category. These are the combinations we see most often:
Product type USA EU Plush toys CPSIA + ASTM F963 + CPC EN 71-1/2/3 + CE + GPSR Plastic figures & dolls CPSIA + ASTM F963 + phthalates + CPC EN 71-1/2/3 + REACH + CE Battery-powered toys Above + UN38.3 + FCC (if wireless) Above + EMC + RoHS + battery regulation Pet toys No CPC required; state-level labeling GPSR + REACH Fidget / sensory (14+) General product safety EN 71 (if marketed to children) If you are unsure which set applies, send the product and target marketplace — we will confirm the exact test package and cost before sampling.

Valid business licence and export rights Existing test reports for comparable products Production capacity against your required delivery date Social-compliance documentation where the buyer’s market requires it (BSCI, Sedex, or equivalent) — availability varies by factory, so we confirm per project rather than assume Packaging and labeling compliance Compliance is not only the product. Age grading and warning statements in the destination language CE / UKCA mark placement per directive Importer name and address (EU GPSR requires this on the label) Batch or lot code for traceability Recycling and battery symbols where applicable We review artwork against these requirements before plates are made, which is far cheaper than reprinting cartons.

Why shipping decides your margin Two sellers can buy the same toy at the same factory price and end up with very different margins. The difference is usually freight: how the goods move, who books it, and whether the cartons are packed to use space efficiently.
We quote logistics as part of the product cost, so you see landed cost rather than a factory price with unknown extras.
EXW vs FOB vs DDP Term You are responsible for Best for Risk EXW (Ex Works) Everything from our warehouse — export clearance, freight, duty Buyers with their own forwarder in China Highest — you own the goods at our door FOB (Free On Board) Ocean freight, insurance, import duty Experienced importers with a freight account Medium — we handle export and loading CIF Import duty and destination charges Buyers who want us to book freight Medium — insurance included, but destination fees can surprise DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) Nothing — we deliver to your address Amazon sellers, small brands, first orders Lowest — one price, one invoice For most first-time buyers and Amazon sellers, DDP is the simplest option: one price that includes freight, duty and delivery, with no surprises at the destination port.
DDP availability depends on destination country and product category. Some markets restrict DDP for certain goods, and duty rates vary by HS code. We confirm feasibility before quoting.
Transit times by destination Sea freight from Ningbo / Shanghai, port to port, excluding customs clearance and inland delivery:
Destination Port Transit time USA West Coast Los Angeles / Long Beach 14 – 20 days USA East Coast New York / Savannah 28 – 36 days Canada Vancouver 16 – 22 days UK Felixstowe / Southampton 30 – 38 days Netherlands Rotterdam 30 – 36 days Germany Hamburg 32 – 38 days Spain Valencia / Barcelona 30 – 36 days France Le Havre / Marseille 30 – 37 days Japan Tokyo / Osaka 4 – 8 days South Korea Busan 3 – 6 days Mexico Manzanillo 20 – 26 days Brazil Santos 35 – 45 days Australia Sydney / Melbourne 16 – 24 days UAE Jebel Ali 18 – 24 days Add 3–7 days for customs clearance at destination, plus inland transport. Actual transit varies with carrier, season and congestion — we confirm the sailing schedule when booking rather than quoting from a static table.
Other modes Mode Transit When it makes sense Air freight 3 – 8 days Urgent restock, high value-to-weight ratio, sample shipments Sea express / LCL 18 – 30 days 1–15 CBM, shared container space Rail (China–Europe) 18 – 25 days EU destinations, faster than sea, cheaper than air Courier (DHL / FedEx) 2 – 5 days Samples only — uneconomical for bulk LCL vs FCL LCL FCL Volume 1 – 15 CBM 20GP ≈ 28 CBM usable, 40HQ ≈ 68 CBM Cost behaviour Per CBM, higher per-unit Fixed per container, lowest per-unit Handling Consolidated, more handling risk Sealed at origin Best for Trial orders, mixed SKUs Repeat orders, single large SKU Where you are between sizes, we calculate both and show the break-even point. A 40HQ is often cheaper per unit than a 20GP once you pass roughly 22 CBM.
Consolidation across suppliers Buying from several factories is normal. Shipping from several is expensive.
We receive goods from multiple factories at our Yiwu warehouse, check quantity and condition on arrival, and consolidate into one shipment — one set of export documents, one container, one freight bill.
This is usually where a sourcing agent pays for itself: consolidating four suppliers into one LCL shipment commonly removes several hundred dollars of freight and handling.
Amazon FBA preparation For FBA sellers we prepare cartons to Amazon’s requirements:
FNSKU label application, or poly-bagging with the required suffocation warning Carton weight and size limits checked per marketplace “Sold as set” / “This is a set” labeling where applicable Shipping plan carton labels and pallet configuration Carton content and quantity reporting back to you before dispatch Requirements differ by marketplace and change periodically. We confirm current specifications against your Seller Central shipping plan before packing, rather than working from last year’s rules.
Packaging for ocean transit Toys ship badly when cartons are built for retail rather than for a container:
Master carton burst strength matched to stacking height Inner boxes to protect retail packaging from compression Moisture protection for long sea routes and humid destinations Drop-test verification on the packed carton, not the bare product We check carton configuration against the product’s fragility and the route before the order is packed.
Documents you receive Document Purpose Commercial invoice & packing list Customs clearance Bill of lading / airway bill Title and transport record Certificate of origin Duty reduction under trade agreements where applicable Test reports & CPC / CE DoC Market access Loading photos & container seal number Proof of condition at dispatch Track your shipment We send a loading report with photographs the day the container leaves, and share carrier tracking until delivery. You are not left guessing whether the goods were actually shipped.

Yes. LCL from 1 CBM, and courier for samples. There is no minimum container requirement.
Who handles customs clearance? Under DDP we handle it end to end. Under FOB or EXW, your forwarder clears the goods and we supply the export documents.
Do you ship to Amazon FBA directly? Yes, including appointment booking where the marketplace requires it. Send the warehouse code and shipping plan and we prepare cartons to spec.
What if the goods arrive damaged? We photograph and record the container seal at loading, which establishes condition at dispatch. If damage occurs in transit, that record supports the insurance claim. Packaging-related damage caused by our carton spec is our responsibility.
Can I combine toys with non-toy products? Usually yes, provided the combined shipment clears the same customs requirements. Tell us the mix and we will confirm before quoting.
